history.heading: Navigators and colonisers
paragraphs: The Marshall Islands consist of 29 coral atolls and 5 islands in two chains in the central Pacific. Micronesian settlers arrived around 2,000 years ago or more and became expert navigators, using stick charts to map ocean swells.
The islands are named after British captain John Marshall, who passed in 1788. Germany annexed them in 1885, and Japan took control in 1914. US forces captured them during fierce battles in 1944.

history.heading: Nuclear testing and independence
paragraphs: After the war the islands became part of the US-administered Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. Between 1946 and 1958 the United States conducted 67 nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak atolls, including the 1954 Castle Bravo test, the largest US nuclear explosion, which contaminated inhabited islands. Bikini's people were displaced and still cannot safely return.
The Marshall Islands became self-governing in 1979 and independent in 1986 under a Compact of Free Association with the United States.

culture.heading: Marshallese life
paragraphs: Marshallese and English are official. Society is matrilineal, with land passed through the mother's line, and chiefs (iroij) remain important. Most people are Protestant Christians. Traditional skills include canoe-building, weaving and navigation.

politics.heading: Free association
paragraphs: The Marshall Islands is a parliamentary republic in which parliament (the Nitijela) elects the president. Under the Compact of Free Association, the US provides funding and defence, and Marshallese can live and work in the United States; a renewed compact was agreed in 2023. The US military operates a missile testing range at Kwajalein. The country recognises Taiwan.

economy.heading: Aid and fishing
paragraphs: The economy depends heavily on US assistance, fishing licences, and revenue from its ship registry, one of the largest in the world. Copra is exported. Many Marshallese have moved to the US, especially Arkansas.
Rising sea levels pose an existential threat, as most land is only about two metres above sea level. The currency is the US dollar.
